description: The honest truth first: IELTS 7+ demands solid B2+ English — technique alone doesn't substitute. This module stacks on Modules 1–4 and teaches you how examiners actually score the test.

steps.body: Dear Tanqeel, this lesson is a promise of honesty, not a promise of magic. **IELTS Band 7+ requires solid B2+ English.** No technique, template, or "examiner trick" substitutes for real language ability. Anyone who sells you Band 7 in 30 days from A2/B1 is selling you a story.

The realistic path is: **6–9 months of foundation** (Modules 1–4 of this course: fluency, accuracy, pronunciation, client communication) **plus 6–8 weeks of IELTS technique.** This module is the technique part. It does not replace the foundation — it converts your foundation into a score. Technique adds roughly one band to the level you actually have; it never adds three.
steps.heading: The realistic path

steps.body: **Listening** — 30 min, 4 sections, 40 questions. **Reading** — 60 min, 3 passages, 40 questions. **Writing** — 60 min: Task 1 (150 words, ~20 min) + Task 2 (250 words, ~40 min). **Speaking** — 11–14 min: Part 1 (4–5 min, familiar topics), Part 2 (3–4 min, cue card talk), Part 3 (4–5 min, discussion). Each section is scored 0–9 in half bands; your overall band is the average.
steps.heading: What the test actually is

steps.body: Band 7 = **"good user"** — operational command with occasional inaccuracies and misunderstandings. Roughly: **30–32/40 in Listening or Reading ≈ Band 7** (varies slightly per test). In Writing and Speaking, Band 7 means you satisfy all four band descriptors with strengths outweighing weaknesses. There is no secret. There is only skill + strategy.
steps.heading: What Band 7 actually means

steps.body: Technique tumhare actual level par **ek band tak** ka izaafa de sakti hai — teen band nahi. Pehle Modules 1–4 se apni English B2 tak le jao, phir ye module tumhein 6.5 se 7.5 tak pohnchayega. Yehi honest rasta hai, aur yehi kaam karta hai.
steps.heading: Sachai (seedhi baat)

steps.prompt:
**Your IELTS baseline (honesty = strategy)**

Write 5 sentences, no exaggeration:
1. Why do you want IELTS? (study abroad? immigration? job?)
2. What band do you NEED vs what band would be nice?
3. Which section scares you most and why?
4. How many real study hours per week can you give for 8 weeks?
5. One foundation skill from Modules 1–4 you must fix first.
Read it back: if any sentence fakes your level, rewrite it. A strategy built on an honest baseline beats a fantasy plan every time.

steps.answer: Task 2 is worth twice as much as Task 1.
steps.explanation: Writing Task 2 counts double — that's why it gets 40 of your 60 minutes.
steps.title: Test facts in order

steps.body: IELTS Listening is not hard because of speed — it's hard because of **traps**. The recording is designed to make confident answers wrong. Three traps account for most lost marks: **distractors** (the answer changes — *"Oh wait, I meant Friday, not Thursday"*), **paraphrase answers** (the question says *"cost"* but the audio says *"price"* — you must recognize synonyms, not match words), and **signpost words** (*"however," "actually," "on the other hand"* — what follows them usually corrects what came before).

You get time before each section. Never waste it: **read the questions first and predict the answer type** — a number? a date? a name? a noun? If question 3 asks *"The course starts in ___"* you predict a month/date, and your ear is already tuned to date-shaped sounds. Prediction turns listening from a memory test into a **confirmation task** — you're just checking whether what you hear matches your guess.
steps.heading: The prediction technique (read first, guess, then listen)

steps.body: **Numbers:** *"fifteen"* vs *"fifty"* — in fast speech the difference is one tiny vowel; always double-check by context. **Dates:** *"the 17th of July"* — write *17 July* or *July 17*, either is accepted, but 17/07/2026 can be marked wrong in some formats. **Spelling:** Section 1 always has a name spelled aloud — write it EXACTLY as dictated, letter by letter. One wrong letter = zero. Capital letters don't matter; correct letters do.
steps.heading: Number, date & spelling traps

steps.body: You get 10 minutes at the end to transfer answers. Use them: check **grammar** (is it singular or plural? *"two book"* → *"two books"*), check **spelling**, and never leave a blank — **there is no negative marking.** A guess has a chance; a blank has none.
steps.heading: Transfer time discipline

steps.explanation: "Sorry" is a signpost — what follows corrects what came before. Always take the corrected answer.
steps.prompt: Audio: "The seminar is on Wednesday... sorry, Thursday." What do you write?
steps.title: Trap spotting

steps.explanation: Use context to resolve unclear sounds — and never leave blanks; there's no negative marking.

steps.body: First, a shadowing drill with the Section 1 audio (a hotel booking conversation). If the audio file isn't on your device yet, use the **read-along script** below: read it aloud twice at natural speed, have a friend read the receptionist's lines while you play the guest — or record yourself reading both parts and quiz yourself from the recording. The questions after it are the real exercise either way.
steps.heading: How this drill works

steps.text: Shadow the booking conversation — receptionist and guest
steps.tip: First pass: just listen. Second pass: shadow the guest. Third: shadow the receptionist. Then answer the 10 questions below.
steps.title: Section 1: hotel booking (audio)

steps.body:
RECEPTIONIST: Good morning, Grandview Hotel. How can I help you?
GUEST: Hi, I'd like to book a room for next week — arriving on the 17th of July.
RECEPTIONIST: The 17th of July... and how many nights will that be?
GUEST: Three nights. Oh wait — actually make it four. We'll leave on the 21st.
RECEPTIONIST: Four nights, 17th to 21st July. And what name is the booking under?
GUEST: Khalid — K-H-A-L-I-D, Mahmood — M-A-H-M-O-O-D.
RECEPTIONIST: Got it, Mr Mahmood. A single or double room?
GUEST: A double, please. Sea view if you have one.
RECEPTIONIST: We have a double with a sea view at 85 dollars a night. Breakfast is included.
GUEST: Perfect. Do you have parking?
RECEPTIONIST: We do — underground parking, 10 dollars per night. Actually, it's free for stays of four nights or more.
GUEST: Great, we'll need one space. My number is 07955 342 118.
RECEPTIONIST: 07955 342 118. And an email for the confirmation?
GUEST: k.mahmood at fastmail dot com.
RECEPTIONIST: You're all set. Check-in is from 2 pm, and check-out is at 11... sorry, 12 noon.
GUEST: 12 noon, got it. Thanks!

steps.body: Reading has 3 passages, 40 questions, **60 minutes — and no extra transfer time.** That means ~20 minutes per passage, no negotiation. Most Band 6 candidates fail on time, not on English. So the #1 strategy is a reading method that stops you from reading the whole passage.

**Skim** = read for structure, not detail: title, first sentence of each paragraph, last paragraph. 90 seconds. You should be able to say: "This passage is about X; paragraph 2 gives history, paragraph 3 gives problems." **Scan** = hunt for one specific word or number in the question, then find its paraphrase in the text. You never read top-to-bottom; you **skim for the map, then scan for the treasure.**
steps.heading: Skim vs scan (the only reading method you need)

steps.body: **TRUE** = the text says exactly this (paraphrased). **FALSE** = the text directly contradicts it. **NOT GIVEN** = the text neither confirms nor denies it. The trap: if the passage says *"the library opens at 9"* and the question says *"the library opens at 9 and is free"* — that's NOT GIVEN, not TRUE. Part of it matches, part is unknown. **Rule of thumb: if you're "sure it's probably true" — it's NOT GIVEN.** TRUE requires text evidence; FALSE requires text contradiction.
steps.heading: The NOT GIVEN trap — the #1 score killer

steps.body:
Short passage — read it once (skim), then answer the 6 questions by scanning:

**Urban rooftops**
A. In 2018, the city of Oslo required all new buildings over 500 m² to include a green roof. The policy aimed to reduce flooding and improve air quality.
B. Early results disappointed engineers. Many roofs planted with grass needed constant watering, and in 2021 the council admitted maintenance costs were higher than expected.
C. Researchers then tested native wildflower mixes. These needed almost no watering and attracted bees. By 2023, wildflower roofs were cheaper to maintain than grass roofs, though the city has not published exact savings figures.
D. Architect Lina Berg argues the real value is psychological: residents report feeling calmer. No clinical study has confirmed this, she admits, but she believes green roofs make cities more humane.
steps.heading: Practice passage: Urban rooftops

steps.explanation: Paragraph A: "all new buildings over 500 m²" — matches. TRUE needs text evidence, and it's there.
steps.prompt: 1. Oslo requires green roofs on all new buildings over 500 m².
steps.title: T/F/NG practice

steps.explanation: Paragraph B: "the council admitted maintenance costs were higher than expected" — direct contradiction of "lower". FALSE.
steps.prompt: 2. Early green roofs were cheaper to maintain than expected.
steps.title: T/F/NG practice

steps.explanation: Paragraph C says wildflower roofs were cheaper but "the city has not published exact savings figures" — we can't confirm 40%. NOT GIVEN.
steps.prompt: 3. Wildflower roofs save the city exactly 40% on maintenance.
steps.title: T/F/NG practice

steps.explanation: Paragraph D: Berg reports residents "feeling calmer" but "no clinical study has confirmed this". Claimed, not proven — NOT GIVEN.
steps.prompt: 4. Green roofs have proven health benefits.
steps.title: T/F/NG practice

steps.explanation: Paragraph C: wildflower mixes "needed almost no watering" — the opposite of constant watering. FALSE.
steps.prompt: 5. Wildflower roofs need constant watering.
steps.title: T/F/NG practice

steps.explanation: The passage never mentions a year for the wildflower tests, only results by 2023. NOT GIVEN.
steps.prompt: 6. Wildflower roof tests began in 2020.
steps.title: T/F/NG practice

steps.body: A heading summarizes the **main idea of a whole paragraph** — ignore details, ask "what is this paragraph mostly FOR?" Paragraph B = problems with early grass roofs. Paragraph C = a better solution (wildflowers). Paragraph D = a claimed psychological benefit. **Trap:** headings reuse words from the passage. Match ideas, not words — if you match the word "bees" you picked the detail, not the main idea.
steps.heading: Matching headings: match ideas, not words

steps.body:
- Passage 1: 17 min (save time on the easy one)
- Passage 2: 20 min
- Passage 3: 23 min (hardest — steal time from Passage 1)
- **If a question eats 2 minutes, guess and move.** A skipped easy question later costs the same mark as a solved hard one now.
- Answer every question — no negative marking.
steps.heading: The 20-minute rule (timing strategy)

steps.explanation: 17 + 20 + 23 = 60, with the hardest passage getting the most time. Discipline beats brilliance.
steps.prompt: Which split fits the 60-minute limit?
steps.title: Timing drill

lessons.title: Reading: skim, scan, and the NOT GIVEN trap

steps.body: Writing Task 1 is a **report, not an essay.** 150+ words, ~20 minutes. You describe what you see: trends, comparisons, processes. **Task 2 counts double**, so Task 1 must be efficient, not beautiful.

- **Line graphs:** *"rose sharply / increased gradually / peaked at / remained stable / fell slightly / fluctuated."*
- **Bar charts:** comparisons — *"twice as high as," "the highest," "slightly more than."*
- **Pie charts:** proportions — *"accounted for 40%," "made up a quarter of," "the smallest share."*
- **Tables:** pick the biggest differences, ignore the rest. Never describe every number.
- **Maps (before/after):** *"was replaced by," "was converted into," "was demolished to make way for," "remained unchanged."*
- **Process diagrams:** passive + sequencers — *"The beans are harvested, then they are dried..."* Use *"first, next, after that, finally."*
steps.heading: Frameworks: trend language for each chart type

steps.body: Every Task 1 needs 4 paragraphs: **(1) Paraphrase** the question (one sentence). **(2) Overview** — the 2–3 most important trends, NO numbers. **(3) Detail 1** (with numbers). **(4) Detail 2** (with numbers). **The overview paragraph IS the band score.** Examiners decide your Task Achievement band from it. If you skip the overview or fill it with numbers, you cap yourself at Band 6.
steps.heading: The 4-paragraph structure — the overview is the band score

steps.body:
*The line graph shows average monthly temperatures in a coastal city and an inland city in 2023.*

**Model answer (Band 8):**
*"The line graph compares monthly average temperatures in a coastal city and an inland city during 2023. **(1 — paraphrase)** Overall, the inland city experienced greater temperature variation throughout the year, while the coastal city remained relatively stable. Temperatures in both cities were lowest in January and highest in July. **(2 — overview: two trends, zero numbers)** In January, the coastal city averaged 8°C compared to just 2°C inland. Both cities warmed steadily until July, when the inland city peaked at 28°C, 6 degrees higher than the coastal city. **(3 — detail 1)** From August onwards, temperatures fell in both locations, though the decline was sharper inland, dropping to 4°C by December, while the coast eased down to 9°C. **(4 — detail 2)**"*
**Annotations:** (1) paraphrase changes every key word (shows→compares). (2) Overview = 2 trends, no data — this paragraph earns Task Achievement. (3–4) data grouped logically (rise, then fall), not month by month. Vocabulary: *peaked, eased, sharper* — variety, not repetition of "increased/decreased."
steps.heading: Model Band 8 answer (annotated)

steps.body: Band 6 Task 1 answers all share three flaws: (1) **no overview** — they start listing numbers immediately; (2) **mechanical description** — *"In January it was 8. In February it was 9..."* (examiners call this "listing"); (3) **opinions** — *"This is good because..."* Task 1 has no opinions. Report only.
steps.heading: Common Band 6 traps

steps.answer: Overview paragraph: the 2–3 key trends, no numbers
steps.explanation: The overview earns Task Achievement; data goes in detail paragraphs.
steps.hint: The band score lives in one paragraph — which?
steps.title: Fix the structure
steps.wrong: Task 1 needs introduction, then numbers for every month, then a conclusion with my opinion.

steps.explanation: "Peaked at" is precise trend vocabulary; Band 7+ rewards exact verbs.
steps.prompt: Which sentence shows Band 7+ trend language?
steps.title: Trend language

steps.answer: The wheat is harvested, then it is transported to the mill, where it is ground into flour.
steps.explanation: Process diagrams: passive voice + sequencers. No "they do" — the focus is the material, not the people.
steps.title: Process diagram sentence
steps.wrong: First they harvest the wheat then they transport to mill.

lessons.title: Writing Task 1: describe data like an examiner

steps.body:
Task 2 is the heavyweight: **250+ words, 40 minutes, worth double.** One prompt, one essay, four types you must recognize instantly:
1. **Opinion** (*"To what extent do you agree or disagree?"*) — take ONE clear position, defend it. Never "I partly agree" wishy-washy... actually a balanced position is fine IF clearly stated and defended.
2. **Discussion** (*"Discuss both views and give your opinion."*) — both sides fairly, then YOUR view in the conclusion.
3. **Problem–solution** (*"What are the causes and what can be done?"*) — one paragraph causes, one paragraph solutions.
4. **Two-part** (*"Why is this happening? Is it positive or negative?"*) — answer EACH part in its own paragraph.

Every body paragraph follows **PEEL**: **P**oint — one clear idea (*"Online learning reduces costs."*). **E**xplain — why/how (*"Students avoid transport and accommodation expenses..."*). **E**xample — specific (*"A student in Multan can study at a university in Lahore without relocating."*). **L**ink — back to the question (*"This makes higher education accessible to poorer families."*). One paragraph = one idea. Two ideas in one paragraph is how Band 6 essays die.
steps.heading: PEEL: one paragraph, one idea

steps.body: Band 6 writers write *"however"* 12 times. Band 7+ writers rotate the toolkit: **contrast** — *however, nevertheless, on the other hand, whereas, in contrast*; **cause** — *because, since, as a result of, this leads to*; **addition** — *furthermore, moreover, in addition*; **example** — *for instance, namely*; **conclusion** — *therefore, consequently, in summary*. One device per idea, then a different one. Variety IS the Cohesion score.
steps.heading: Cohesion devices (not "however" spam)

steps.body: Examiners reward three grammar shapes: **conditionals** (*"If governments invested in public transport, cities would be cleaner."*), **relative clauses** (*"Students **who** study online often save money."*), **passive** (*"Data **is collected** from millions of users."*). Aim for 2–3 of each across the essay. They prove "grammatical range" — half your Grammar band.
steps.heading: High-band grammar: the big three

steps.body:
*"Some people believe online education will replace traditional classrooms. To what extent do you agree or disagree?"*

**Model answer (Band 8–9):**
*"Online education has grown rapidly, leading some to claim that physical classrooms will soon disappear. **(1 — position in intro)** I largely disagree: while online learning offers real advantages, it cannot replace the social and practical dimensions of classroom education. **(2 — clear position)** The strongest argument for online learning is access. Students in remote areas, **who** previously had no options, can now study with top instructors. **(3 — relative clause)** For instance, a student in rural Pakistan can complete a data science degree without moving to a big city, which dramatically reduces costs. **(4 — example)** Nevertheless **(5 — cohesion variety)**, education is not only information transfer. Classrooms build discipline, teamwork, and communication — skills **that** employers consistently demand. **(6)** If learning moved entirely online **(7 — conditional)**, millions of students would lose daily human interaction, and the motivation that comes from peer pressure would weaken. In conclusion, online education is a powerful supplement, but it should complement rather than replace traditional classrooms. **(8 — restated position, no new ideas)**"*
**Annotations:** (1–2) position stated twice, never vague. (3–4) PEEL: point → who-clause → specific example. (5) *nevertheless* not *however*. (7) conditional for the Band 7+ grammar tick. (8) conclusion restates, adds nothing new — a classic Band 6 mistake avoided.
steps.heading: Model Band 8–9 essay (annotated)

steps.body: (1) **Memorized phrases** — *"In this contemporary era of globalization..."* Examiners spot templates instantly and penalize them. (2) **New ideas in the conclusion.** (3) **No position** — sitting on the fence for 250 words. (4) **Under-length** — below 250 words = automatic Task Achievement penalty, however good the English. (5) **Over-generalizing** — *"All students prefer online learning."* Use *"many / most / some"* qualifiers.
steps.heading: Common Band 6 traps

steps.body:
Score any practice essay with the examiner's four criteria, simplified:
- [ ] **Task achievement:** Did I answer ALL parts? 250+ words? Clear position throughout?
- [ ] **Coherence & cohesion:** PEEL paragraphs? One idea each? Cohesion devices varied (not however ×10)? Logical order?
- [ ] **Lexical resource:** Topic vocabulary used naturally? Collocations (*"reduce costs," "gain access"*)? Any word repeated 5+ times? No memorized phrases?
- [ ] **Grammatical range & accuracy:** 2+ conditionals? Relative clauses? Passive? Errors rare and don't block meaning?
One honest "no" = one band lost. Fix the no, not the whole essay.
steps.heading: Self-scoring rubric: Writing (the examiner's checklist)

steps.answer: PEEL: one clear point, explained, with a specific example, linked back to the question
steps.explanation: One paragraph = one idea. PEEL enforces it.
steps.title: Fix the paragraph
steps.wrong: Good body paragraphs just need many ideas and long sentences to impress the examiner.

steps.explanation: A fence-sitting essay scores Band 6 for Task Achievement. Take a position and defend it.
options: "I partly agree with both sides and everyone is right."
"I largely agree: online learning expands access, though classrooms still matter."
steps.prompt: Which intro line shows a clear position?
steps.title: Position drill

steps.answer: If governments invested in public transport, cities would be cleaner and less congested.
steps.explanation: Second conditional: If + past, would + verb. A Band 7+ grammar shape.
steps.title: Build the conditional
steps.wrong: If government invest in public transport, cities will be more clean.

steps.body: **Part 1 (4–5 min):** familiar topics — home, studies, hobbies. The examiner wants natural, extended answers. Formula: **Answer + Reason + Example.** *"Do you like reading?"* → *"Yes, I do **(answer)** — mostly non-fiction, because I enjoy learning how things work **(reason)**. I just finished a book on data science, actually **(example)**."* One-word answers = Band 5. This formula alone lifts most candidates a full band.

You get a topic card + **1 minute to prepare** + **2 minutes to talk**. Method: (1) Use the minute — write 5–6 keywords, not sentences. Shorthand: "cabin — lake — quiet — stars — 2024". (2) Talk for the full 2 minutes using this structure: **past** (when/where it happened) → **description** (what it was like, 2–3 details) → **feeling + why** (how it affected you). (3) If you finish early, the examiner stays silent — keep going: add one more detail. Never stop at 90 seconds.
steps.heading: Part 2: the cue-card method (1-min prep, 2-min talk)

steps.body: **Part 3 (4–5 min):** abstract discussion linked to your Part 2 topic. The examiner wants **balanced views**: *"On the one hand... on the other hand..."*, *"It depends on..."*, *"Generally speaking..."* Structure: **opinion → reason → contrast/other side → conclusion.** *"Will technology replace teachers?"* → *"I don't think so entirely (opinion) — teaching is partly emotional connection (reason). That said, for rote subjects like vocabulary, apps are already better (contrast). So technology will assist, not replace (conclusion)."*
steps.heading: Part 3: discussion with balanced views

steps.text: Shadow a full Part 2 cue-card answer — copy the structure, not just the words
steps.tip: Notice the past → description → feeling structure. Then record your own 2-minute answer on the same topic.
steps.title: Part 2 model answer (audio)

steps.body:
Score any practice recording with the examiner's four criteria, simplified:
- [ ] **Fluency & coherence:** Did I speak at length without long pauses? Ideas in logical order? Self-corrections rare?
- [ ] **Lexical resource:** Topic vocabulary? Collocations? Any word I leaned on 10+ times? Paraphrasing when stuck instead of freezing?
- [ ] **Grammatical range & accuracy:** Mix of simple and complex sentences? Past/present/future used correctly? Errors don't block understanding?
- [ ] **Pronunciation:** Word stress right? Sentence stress on key words? Could a stranger understand me first time?
Record → score honestly → re-record the weakest 60 seconds. That loop is the whole method.
steps.heading: Self-scoring rubric: Speaking (the examiner's checklist)

steps.prompt: Part 2 cue card: "Describe a skill you would like to learn." You should say: what the skill is, why you want to learn it, how you would learn it — and explain how it would help you in the future. 1 minute prep (5–6 keywords only), then talk for 2 full minutes. Record it. Score yourself with the Speaking rubric above, honestly.
steps.tip: Past → description → feeling. Keep talking when the examiner goes silent.

steps.body: Full Mock A. Work it under **exam conditions**: no pausing, no dictionary, timer on. Do the listening questions first (imagine the audio plays once), then reading (20 min), then write both tasks (60 min), then record the speaking. Answer keys live in the explanations — attempt before peeking.

**LISTENING — Section 2: Museum tour (script)**
GUIDE: Welcome to the Riverside Museum. Before we start, a few practical details. We open at 10 am... actually, on weekends it's 9:30. The main exhibition is on the ground floor. The café is on the top floor — the third floor — and it's open until 4 pm. Photography is allowed everywhere except the special exhibition room. Today's guided tour costs 12 pounds for adults — oh, I should say 10 pounds; we reduced the price this month. Children under 12 go free. The tour takes about 90 minutes. We finish in the gift shop on the first floor. Any questions? No? Then let's begin in the main hall — straight through those doors.

steps.body:
**READING — Passage: "The return of the night train"**
A. For decades, night trains across Europe were disappearing. Cheap flights made them uneconomical, and by 2016 several countries had cancelled their last sleeper services.
B. Then the mood shifted. Climate concern made flying feel guilty, and in 2021 Austria's state railway reported sleeper bookings up 30% on 2019. New routes opened: Vienna–Paris, Zurich–Amsterdam.
C. The economics remain difficult. A sleeper carriage costs far more to run than a daytime seat, and tickets must stay cheap enough to compete with budget airlines. Operators survive on a mix of ticket sales and state subsidies.
D. Critics argue night trains will always be a niche. Supporters counter that niches matter: even a 5% shift from planes to trains on short European routes would cut aviation emissions measurably.

steps.body:
**WRITING TASK 1 (20 min, 150+ words):** The bar chart below shows the percentage of households with internet access in four countries in 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

**Model answer (Band 8):** *"The bar chart compares household internet access in four countries in 2010 and 2020. (paraphrase) Overall, access rose in every country over the decade, with Country A remaining the clear leader throughout. (overview — trend + leader, no numbers) In 2010, 80% of households in Country A had internet, roughly double the figure for Country D at 40%. Countries B and C sat in the middle at 55% and 60%. (detail 1 — 2010 snapshot) By 2020, Country A had reached near-universal access at 95%, while Country D had more than doubled to 85%, the fastest growth of the four. Countries B and C also climbed steadily to 78% and 82%. (detail 2 — 2020 + change)"*
**Annotations:** overview = 2 trends, zero numbers. Details grouped by year (2010, then 2020), not by country. Language: *near-universal, fastest growth, climbed steadily.*
steps.heading: Mock A — Writing Task 1 + model answer

steps.body:
**WRITING TASK 2 (40 min, 250+ words):** Some people think that university education should be free for all students. Others believe students should pay for their own tuition. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

**Model answer (Band 8–9):** *"Whether higher education should be free is one of the most debated policy questions of our time. (paraphrase) This essay will discuss both perspectives before arguing that a mixed system is fairest. (roadmap) Supporters of free university argue that talent is evenly distributed but opportunity is not. (point) If tuition were free (conditional), bright students from poor families could study medicine or engineering instead of taking low-paid jobs at eighteen. (explain + example) Countries like Germany, which abolished tuition fees, have seen wider participation without collapsing quality. (evidence) On the other hand, critics point out that free university is expensive for taxpayers, many of whom never attend. (other view) They argue that graduates earn significantly more over their lifetimes, so it is reasonable for them to contribute through fees or graduate taxes. (explain) In my opinion, the fairest model combines both: free tuition for students from low-income families, funded partly by contributions from higher earners after graduation. (clear position) This keeps opportunity open while sharing costs fairly. (link) In conclusion, while both sides raise valid concerns, a targeted free-tuition system best balances fairness and sustainability. (restated position, no new ideas)"*
**Annotations:** discussion type — both views fairly, own opinion clearly in body + conclusion. PEEL in each paragraph. Conditional + relative clause (*"which abolished"*). Position never vague.
steps.heading: Mock A — Writing Task 2 + model answer

TUTOR: So, Aisha, your proposal for the water-quality project. You've chosen the river site?
AISHA: Yes — the north bank. I first thought about the south bank, but the readings there were... actually, the north bank had higher pollution levels in last year's survey.

steps.body:
**READING — Passage: "Why waiting feels longer than it is"**
A. Psychologists have long known that perceived waiting time differs from clock time. A two-minute wait can feel like ten if the conditions are wrong.
B. The key factor is uncertainty. In a famous 2018 experiment, passengers told their bus would arrive "soon" estimated the wait as twice as long as passengers given an exact countdown. Information, it seems, shortens time.
C. Occupied time also feels shorter. Airports discovered that passengers complained less about baggage delays after walkways to the carousel were lengthened — the walk filled the wait.
D. However, not all distractions help. A 2022 study found that phone scrolling during waits increased frustration, possibly because it raised expectations of constant stimulation.

steps.body:
**WRITING TASK 1 (20 min, 150+ words):** The table below shows the percentage of household income spent on four categories in three countries in 2022. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

**Model answer (Band 8):** *"The table compares how households in three countries allocated their income across four categories in 2022. (paraphrase) Overall, housing was the largest expense in all three countries, while spending on entertainment was consistently the smallest. Country X devoted the highest share to housing, whereas Country Z spent relatively more on food. (overview — two patterns, no numbers) In Country X, housing absorbed 32% of income, compared with 28% in Country Y and 25% in Country Z. Food showed the reverse pattern: Country Z spent 22%, noticeably more than Country X at 15%. (detail 1) Transport costs were similar everywhere, ranging from 12% to 14%, and entertainment accounted for just 6–8% in all three countries, the lowest share in each case. (detail 2)"*
**Annotations:** table strategy — pick the biggest differences, ignore the rest. Overview first, numbers only in details. Comparatives (*higher, noticeably more*) carry the Cohesion score.
steps.heading: Mock B — Writing Task 1 + model answer

steps.body:
**WRITING TASK 2 (40 min, 250+ words):** Some people believe that children should learn a foreign language at primary school rather than secondary school. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

**Model answer (Band 8–9):** *"At what age children should begin learning foreign languages is widely debated. (paraphrase) I strongly agree that primary school is the better starting point, for reasons of brain development and long-term motivation. (clear position) Young children acquire pronunciation far more naturally than teenagers. (point) Research on language acquisition shows that the ability to hear and reproduce unfamiliar sounds declines after roughly age twelve. (explain) A child who starts English at seven, therefore, is more likely to develop a natural accent than one who begins at fourteen. (example + link) Furthermore (cohesion variety), early success builds confidence. (point) A ten-year-old who can already hold a simple conversation feels capable, and this sense of achievement sustains motivation through the harder grammar of later years. (explain) If language learning is delayed until secondary school (conditional), many students associate it only with exams and memorisation, which kills interest. (contrast) Admittedly, primary curricula are already crowded. (concession) However, language games and songs take little time and suit young learners perfectly. (rebuttal) In conclusion, starting foreign languages in primary school gives children a lasting advantage in both pronunciation and motivation. (restated position)"*
**Annotations:** opinion type — one clear position defended throughout. PEEL in each paragraph. Concession + rebuttal (*admittedly... however*) = Band 8 discussion skill. Conditional for grammar range.

steps.title: Quiz — IELTS Mastery

steps.body:
- [ ] I can name the three Listening traps (distractors, paraphrase, signposts) and use the prediction technique
- [ ] I skim for structure and scan for answers; I never read a passage top-to-bottom
- [ ] I apply T/F/NG logic without upgrading guesses to TRUE
- [ ] My Task 1 has a real overview paragraph (trends, no numbers) in 4 paragraphs
- [ ] My Task 2 takes a clear position, uses PEEL paragraphs, varied cohesion devices, and 2+ high-band grammar shapes
- [ ] I can extend Part 1 answers (Answer+Reason+Example), run the Part 2 cue-card method, and give balanced Part 3 views
- [ ] I can self-score any writing or speaking performance with the examiner checklists
steps.heading: Can-do statements

steps.body: Record one **full Speaking mock** — Parts 1, 2, and 3, 11–14 minutes, no stopping: Part 1 (5 questions on a familiar topic, Answer+Reason+Example), Part 2 (a fresh cue card: "Describe a place you would like to visit" — 1 min prep, 2 min talk), Part 3 (4 discussion questions, balanced views). Then score it with the Speaking rubric from Lesson 7. This recording is your IELTS baseline artifact — redo it after 8 weeks of technique practice and compare.
steps.heading: Mini-test (the final exam)

steps.body:
Technique decays without use. One full mock per month keeps it alive: redo Mock A or B under exam conditions, and re-record the Speaking mock. When your self-scores stop rising, your foundation (Modules 1–4) needs the work — technique has done its job.

🎓 **Badge earned: Band Hunter** — technique is yours. Now go build the B2+ foundation it multiplies.
